summary.text: Lucas congruences pair the terms indexed by \(k\) and \(p+k\), proving both sums vanish modulo \(p\) for \(p\le n\le2p-2\); at \(n=p-1\), \(\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k\) gives the first value \(1\), while the central-binomial factors leave only \(k=(p-1)/2\) in the second sum, giving \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\). Thus both Hankel matrices are anti-triangular modulo \(p\), and multiplying their constant anti-diagonal entries by the reversal permutation’s sign \((-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\) yields the two claimed residues.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                         \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and put
\[
m=\frac{p-1}{2},
\qquad\text{so that}\qquad p=2m+1.
\]
All congruences in the proof are modulo \(p\), or equivalently identities in the field \(\mathbb F_p\).

We shall prove four facts:

1. \(a(n)\equiv0\) for \(p\le n\le2p-2\);
2. \(c(n)\equiv0\) for \(p\le n\le2p-2\);
3. \(a(p-1)\equiv1\);
4. \(c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m\).

These facts make the two Hankel matrices anti-triangular modulo \(p\), after which their determinants can be read from their anti-diagonals.

We repeatedly use the following one-step form of Lucas's theorem. For nonnegative integers \(N,K\),
\[
 \binom NK\equiv
 \binom{N\bmod p}{K\bmod p}
 \binom{\lfloor N/p\rfloor}{\lfloor K/p\rfloor}\pmod p.
\tag{1}
\]
In particular, if a base-\(p\) lower digit of \(K\) exceeds the corresponding digit of \(N\), the binomial coefficient vanishes modulo \(p\).

We will also need the following consequence of (1). If \(0\le x<p\), then
\[
 \binom{2p+2x}{p+x}\equiv 2\binom{2x}{x}.
\tag{2}
\]
Indeed, if \(2x<p\), the lower base-\(p\) digits are \(2x,x\), while the upper digits are \(2,1\), so Lucas's theorem gives
\[
 \binom{2p+2x}{p+x}\equiv \binom{2x}{x}\binom21
 =2\binom{2x}{x}.
\]
If \(2x\ge p\), then the lower digit of \(2p+2x\) is \(2x-p<x\). Thus the left side is zero by Lucas's theorem. The same argument applied to \(\binom{2x}{x}\), whose upper lower digit is again \(2x-p<x\), shows that the right side is also zero. This proves (2) in both cases.


### 1. Vanishing of \(a(n)\) above \(p-1\)

Let \(p\le n\le2p-2\), and write
\[
n=p+r,\qquad 0\le r\le p-2.
\]
Terms with \(k>n\) have \(\binom nk=0\), so we may extend the defining sum for \(a(n)\) to all \(0\le k<2p\). Every such \(k\) can be written uniquely as
\[
k=ip+j,\qquad i\in\{0,1\},\quad 0\le j<p.
\]
Lucas's theorem gives
\[
 \binom{p+r}{ip+j}
 \equiv \binom rj\binom1i=\binom rj.
\tag{3}
\]
Because \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{ip+j}=(-1)^{i+j}.
\]
Consequently, for each fixed \(j\), the contributions corresponding to \(i=0\) and \(i=1\) are
\[
 (-1)^j\binom rj^4
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 -(-1)^j\binom rj^4,
\]
and cancel. Therefore
\[
a(n)\equiv0\qquad(p\le n\le2p-2).
\tag{4}
\]


### 2. Vanishing of \(c(n)\) above \(p-1\)

Again write \(n=p+r\), where \(0\le r\le p-2\), and extend the sum defining \(c(n)\) to \(0\le k<2p\); the added terms vanish because \(\binom nk=0\). Pair the term indexed by \(j\) with the one indexed by \(p+j\), for each \(0\le j<p\).

First suppose \(j\le r\). Lucas's theorem gives
\[
 \binom{p+r}{j}\equiv\binom rj,
 \qquad
 \binom{p+r}{p+j}\equiv\binom rj.
\tag{5}
\]
Set
\[
B_x=\binom{2x}{x}.
\]
For \(k=j\), the two central-binomial factors are
\[
 B_j
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \binom{2(p+r-j)}{p+r-j}.
\]
Since \(0\le r-j<p\), formula (2) says that the second factor is congruent to \(2B_{r-j}\). For \(k=p+j\), formula (2) says that the first central-binomial factor is congruent to \(2B_j\), while the second is simply \(B_{r-j}\), because
\[
n-(p+j)=r-j.
\]
Finally, since \(p\) is odd,
\[
(-1)^{p+j}=-(-1)^j.
\]
Thus the two paired summands are congruent to
\[
 (-1)^j\binom rj^2 B_j(2B_{r-j})

a nd

 -(-1)^j\binom rj^2(2B_j)B_{r-j},
\]
respectively, and hence cancel.

If instead \(j>r\), Lucas's theorem gives
\[
\binom{p+r}{j}\equiv\binom rj=0,
\qquad
\binom{p+r}{p+j}\equiv\binom rj=0,
\]
so both members of the pair vanish separately. We conclude that
\[
c(n)\equiv0\qquad(p\le n\le2p-2).
\tag{6}
\]


### 3. The value of \(a(p-1)\)

For \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\binom{p-1}{k}\equiv(-1)^k.
\tag{7}
\]
For completeness, this follows inductively from Pascal's identity. The case \(k=0\) is immediate. For \(0<k<p\), the prime \(p\) divides \(\binom pk\), and Pascal's identity gives
\[
0\equiv\binom pk
 =\binom{p-1}{k-1}+\binom{p-1}{k},
\]
which advances the induction.

Using (7),
\[
a(p-1)
 \equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4
 =\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\]
There are \(p=2m+1\) terms in this alternating sum, so all adjacent pairs cancel and one term remains. Hence
\[
a(p-1)\equiv1.
\tag{8}
\]


### 4. The value of \(c(p-1)\)

We first record a standard central-binomial congruence. For \(0\le k\le m\),
\[
 \binom{2k}{k}\equiv(-4)^k\binom mk.
\tag{9}
\]
One way to see this is to compare the products term by term. Since all integers \(1,\ldots,k\) are invertible modulo \(p\),
\[
(-4)^k\binom mk
 =\prod_{r=0}^{k-1}\frac{-4(m-r)}{r+1}.
\]
Because \(2m=p-1\),
\[
-4(m-r)\equiv2(2r+1)\pmod p.
\]
Therefore
\[
(-4)^k\binom mk
 \equiv\prod_{r=0}^{k-1}\frac{2(2r+1)}{r+1}
 =\binom{2k}{k},
\]
which proves (9).

By (7), the square \(\binom{p-1}{k}^2\) is congruent to \(1\). Hence
\[
c(p-1)\equiv
 \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k
 \binom{2k}{k}
 \binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}.
\tag{10}
\]
We claim that every summand in (10) except the one with \(k=m\) is zero modulo \(p\).

If \(k>m\), then \(p\le2k<2p\), so the lower base-\(p\) digit of \(2k\) is \(2k-p\). Since \(k<p\) and \(2k-p<k\), Lucas's theorem gives
\[
 \binom{2k}{k}\equiv\binom{2k-p}{k}=0.
\tag{11}
\]
If \(k<m\), put \(\ell=p-1-k=2m-k\). Then \(\ell>m\), and applying the same argument to \(\ell\) yields
\[
 \binom{2\ell}{\ell}\equiv0.
\tag{12}
\]
Explicitly, \(p<2\ell<2p\), its lower digit is
\[
2\ell-p=p-2-2k< p-1-k=\ell,
\]
so Lucas's theorem again makes the coefficient zero.

Thus only \(k=m\) survives. Since \(p-1-m=m\), equation (10) becomes
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m\binom{2m}{m}^2.
\tag{13}
\]
By (9), \(\binom{2m}{m}\equiv(-4)^m\). Moreover, Fermat's theorem and \(2m=p-1\) give
\[
(-4)^m=(-1)^m4^m=(-1)^m2^{2m}
=(-1)^m2^{p-1}\equiv(-1)^m.
\tag{14}
\]
Here \(2\not\equiv0\pmod p\), since \(p\) is odd. Squaring (14) gives \(\binom{2m}{m}^2\equiv1\). Hence (13) yields
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m.
\tag{15}
\]


### 5. An anti-triangular determinant formula

We now establish the determinant fact needed for both matrices. Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and let \(M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<p}\) satisfy
\[
M_{ij}=0\qquad\text{whenever }i+j>p-1.
\tag{16}
\]
Then
\[
\det M=(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}M_{i,p-1-i}.
\tag{17}
\]

To prove this directly, expand the determinant by permutations. A term belonging to a permutation \(\sigma\) can be nonzero only if
\[
i+\sigma(i)\le p-1
\qquad(0\le i<p).
\tag{18}
\]
But
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\bigl(i+\sigma(i)\bigr)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}i+\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}\sigma(i)
 =2\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}i
 =p(p-1).
\tag{19}
\]
The sum of the \(p\) upper bounds in (18) is also \(p(p-1)\). Therefore equality must hold in every instance of (18):
\[
i+\sigma(i)=p-1\quad\text{for every }i.
\]
Thus \(\sigma\) is forced to be the reversal permutation
\[
\rho(i)=p-1-i.
\]
All other determinant terms vanish. The reversal permutation has one inversion for every pair \(i<j\), hence \(\binom p2=p(p-1)/2\) inversions and sign \((-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\). Its determinant term is precisely the product of the anti-diagonal entries. This proves (17).


### 6. The determinant formed from \(a(n)\)

Let
\[
A=(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
Reduce all entries modulo \(p\). Since \(0\le i,j<p\), one has \(i+j\le2p-2\). If \(i+j>p-1\), then \(p\le i+j\le2p-2\), so (4) gives
\[
a(i+j)\equiv0.
\]
Thus the reduced matrix satisfies the anti-triangular condition (16). Every anti-diagonal entry has index \(i+(p-1-i)=p-1\), and by (8) equals \(1\). Formula (17) therefore gives
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\tag{20}
\]
Since \(p=2m+1\),
\[
\frac{p(p-1)}2=pm=(2m+1)m\equiv m\pmod2.
\]
Powers of \(-1\) depend only on the parity of the exponent, so (20) becomes
\[
\det A\equiv(-1)^m
 =(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p.
\tag{21}
\]


### 7. The determinant formed from \(c(n)\)

Let
\[
C=(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}.
\]
As before, if \(i+j>p-1\), then \(p\le i+j\le2p-2\), and (6) gives \(c(i+j)\equiv0\). Thus \(C\) is also anti-triangular modulo \(p\).

Every anti-diagonal entry is now, by (15),
\[
c(p-1)\equiv(-1)^m.
\]
There are \(p\) such entries, so (17) yields
\[
\det C
 \equiv(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p.
\]
Because \(p(p-1)/2=pm\), this is
\[
\det C\equiv(-1)^{pm}(-1)^{pm}
 =(-1)^{2pm}=1\pmod p.
\tag{22}
\]

Equations (21) and (22) are exactly the two asserted congruences:
\[
\boxed{\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p}.
\]
